title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
content: Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments. Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton. The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments. The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria. The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954. In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars. Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly. Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music. These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute. When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers. The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design. But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection of the Stratocaster design in Germany. The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections. The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author". It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms". On its website, Fender announced in March the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced". Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe. One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products". The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars. The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians. "Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments. Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole. "We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action." The letter, he says, came as a shock. "For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions." In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier. "As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action." In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape. Thomann says that the Düsseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims". For its part, Fender, which is majority-owned by Hawaii-based company Servco Pacific, says it has a responsibility to protect the Stratocaster's iconic design. In July, it sued Thomann in a German court, for copyright infringement. In a statement to the BBC, Fender said it remained "confident" in the original Düsseldorf court judgement. "Our preference has always been to keep lines of communication open and resolve these matters through constructive dialogue rather than litigation," it added. With the legal cases continuing, Thomann says he believes it is important to get "legal clarity – not only for us but for the wider guitar industry." "Ultimately, we want to help preserve an environment in which innovation, diversity and creative development can continue to thrive," he adds. Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too. "We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says. "Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this." One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away". "They were asking us to retrieve guitars from dealers out there and destroy them and send them proof. "So when we heard Hans Thomann got the same letter and responded by suing them… so that everybody in the guitar community could understand exactly what's going on… we were so thankful and grateful," he says. Fender tells BBC that it agrees that "legal clarity was important", and that it was now focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers. It also says it realises that "our outreach has caused concern and frustration, particularly among smaller, independent guitar builders. "To them we say: we continue to hear you, and we're listening."

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive development in the economy category, specifically a copyright dispute over the iconic Fender Stratocaster guitar design, which has global implications for the music industry and intellectual property law. The story provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it highlights the importance of creative freedom and the impact on small businesses and consumers.

title: Russian oil firm Lukoil’s overseas assets sold to investors led by US billionaire Todd Boehly
content: US billionaire Todd Boehly is leading a consortium to acquire the vast portfolio of international energy assets belonging to Russia’s second-largest oil producer, his investment firm Eldridge announced Wednesday. Eldridge said in a statement that the consortium, which includes the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, had agreed to buy Lukoil International from its sanctioned Russian parent. The sale price was not disclosed, but the deal will result in the US government receiving an equity stake in Lukoil via the DFC. The deal will “secure critical global energy assets under American and allied ownership,” the statement added. Lukoil’s upstream operations span 11 countries and currently produce around 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. The portfolio includes oil and gas fields; three refineries in Europe; 2,000 retail gas stations across 16 countries in Europe, North America and Central Asia; and an international trading business. Lukoil’s overseas portfolio of assets will be acquired via a share swap, with restricted shares in its Russian parent and other Russian companies exchanged for Lukoil International’s equity. This “avoids any direct cash payment to Russia under the transaction,” Eldridge said. Other investment partners include UAE-based Catena Investment Holding and US investment bank Xtellus Partners. The transaction is subject to conditional approval from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. CNN has contacted Lukoil and the DFC for comment. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a defense and security think tank in London, argued that the deal “demonstrates the efficiency of sanctions.” “Western sanctions are forcing one of Russia’s largest oil companies to relinquish international assets accumulated over decades,” Katinas told CNN earlier this month, ahead of the deal being announced. Transferring refineries and fuel stations to non-Russian owners will “reduce Moscow’s trade influence over important energy infrastructure and remove a source of future earnings for Lukoil,” he added. The deal caps a long and tumultuous sale process. Lukoil put its international assets up for sale more than a year ago after the Treasury Department sanctioned the company in a bid to pressure Moscow to end its war in Ukraine by cutting off an important source of revenue. Rosneft, Russia’s top oil producer, was also sanctioned at the time. The months that followed saw potential deals come and go. Last year, Swiss commodities trading firm Gunvor Group, now Centalion, made an offer for the assets—though the deal was scuttled when it could not win approval from the Treasury. Then, in January, private equity firm Carlyle agreed to buy the foreign assets, excluding those in Kazakhstan. That deal also fell apart this year. The transaction is an unusual investment for Boehly, a part-owner of sports teams including the Los Angeles Dodgers and Los Angeles Lakers. Boehly’s asset management and insurance holding company Eldridge, which manages more than $75 billion in assets, is focused mostly on sports, entertainment, diversified credit and real estate.

title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
content: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading. The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower. The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks. Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day. Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower. The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly. Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact. The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy. The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs. But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry. Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off. "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management. Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year. Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%. The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.
